title: Emotion as Context (eCMR)
content_html:
Emotion as Context (eCMR)

Emotion as context (in eCMR) treats affect — primarily arousal, but also valence/task-related affective tags — as part of the drifting internal context that binds items at encoding and is reinstated at retrieval. Emotional events bias attention and neuromodulation, strengthening item↔context bindings and nudging the context state toward emotional features. Later, reinstating those features preferentially cues other items encoded under similar affect, producing emotion-dependent clustering, list-composition effects (emotional items outcompete neutral ones when mixed), and emotional oddball effects. This account complements consolidation accounts by explaining both immediate and delayed advantages via encoding/retrieval dynamics grounded in temporal + emotional context.

Mechanism (conceptual)

  1. Context carries affect: the context vector c is augmented with emotional features (arousal/valence, task-affect cues).
  2. Arousal amplifies binding: heightened arousal engages LC–NE and related systems, increasing attention/priority and strengthening item↔context associations (M updates).
  3. Encoding drift: c drifts toward active emotional features during emotional items or mood states.
  4. Retrieval reinstatement: recalling an emotional item blends its stored emotional context back into c, cueing temporally/affectively similar items (emotion clustering, mood-congruence).
  5. Competition: when lists are mixed, emotional items win more often due to stronger cue match and competitive dynamics (list-composition & oddball effects).

eCMR formalizes (1)–(5) atop CMR/TCM dynamics; arousal-biased competition and LC–NE physiology motivate steps (2)–(3).

Predicted / explained phenomena

  • Emotional list-composition: mixed lists favor emotional items; pure-neutral lists reduce that advantage.
  • Emotional oddball: a single high-arousal item disrupts local temporal organization and is well remembered.
  • Emotion-dependent clustering: recalls cluster by affective category and by time.
  • Immediate and delayed advantages arise without appealing solely to consolidation, via retrieved-context dynamics.
  • Mood/state dependence: inducing an affective state sets initial context and biases which items are cued.

Neural/physiological grounding

Arousal engages the locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC–NE) system and interacts with amygdala–hippocampal circuits, prioritizing salient stimuli (“winner‑take‑more”). This provides a mechanistic route for stronger item↔context binding and for reinstatement to carry emotional features at retrieval.

How it differs from “consolidation‑only” accounts

  • Scope: eCMR explains immediate recall patterns (clustering, oddball disruption) via retrieval dynamics, not just slower consolidation.
  • Predictive knobs: changing arousal during encoding vs retrieval yields distinct signatures (e.g., clustering vs overall strength), which you can test in simulations.
  • Unification: temporal + emotional context under one cueing mechanism; consolidation can still add delayed benefits.
